headline: Anthropic's record IPO has become a stress test for the AI trade and the banks that sold it, as a tech-led selloff spreads into Asia and 7% mortgage rates weigh on housing. Biotech news is mostly FDA setbacks, trial misses and steady dealmaking.
watch: Anthropic's share price against its IPO price when US trading reopens, and any fresh bank commentary on the offering
Asia's open after South Korea's emergency measures and China's lower margin requirement
Hormuz oil flows and whether Iranian strikes keep cutting exports
Any new detail on the reported SEC probe into Nvidia's accounting
The UBS capital vote in parliament, and who is next in line for the FDA commissioner job

paragraphs.text: The sharpest regulatory story is Capricor. The FDA rejected its Duchenne muscular dystrophy cell therapy deramiocel for the second time, even after the company narrowed the indication. BioPharma Dive says the agency made an unusual public statement accusing Capricor of serious data integrity violations that compromised its study findings. STAT calls the decision long expected. For investors, the language is the point: the agency questioned the integrity of the data, not only whether the trial hit its endpoint. Elsewhere, Fierce Pharma Asia says the FDA's complete response letter to Summit and Akeso on ivonescimab listed more complaints than the overall survival miss. Belite Bio's eye disease pill had its FDA decision pushed back three months, to May. On the positive side, Sanofi won approval for Infilbray in Gaucher type 3, billed as the first therapy to address the disease's neurological effects. Novo's Sogroya picked up its fourth label expansion this year.

paragraphs.text: Agency governance is also moving. The FDA's biologics center is creating a safety council to oversee marketed vaccines and cell and gene therapies. Fierce Biotech reports that the White House pulled its FDA commissioner nomination at the last minute, so leadership remains unsettled. The same roundup says Teva's R&D head resigned a week after its R&D day, and that Quanterix restarted its CEO search.

paragraphs.text: On the clinical side, Merck's TROP2-directed antibody-drug conjugate sacituzumab tirumotecan improved overall survival in a phase 3 gastroesophageal cancer trial. Fierce calls it the drug's second pivotal global win. Merck also won legal rulings against Halozyme in the US and Germany over subcutaneous Keytruda Qlex, which clears hurdles for that formulation. Bausch + Lomb and Celldex both reported phase 2 failures. Celldex dropped the indication, while Bausch + Lomb is pointing to numerical improvements and exploratory analyses to argue for phase 3 talks. Evaxion is dropping infectious disease and autoimmune work to focus only on cancer vaccines. Novo is cutting 215 jobs tied to its New Jersey headquarters as it redesigns its US sales organization, and Fierce has started a weekly tracker of the Wegovy pill against Lilly's Foundayo.

paragraphs.text: Deal and financing chatter stayed busy. Axios and Endpoints both point to a roughly $5 billion haul for Isomorphic, though the excerpts give no terms. Axios also says Leo Pharma delayed its IPO and that Lilly keeps shopping for deals. Simply Wall St says Insmed is drawing acquisition interest, but the report is light on detail and names no bidder. Pfizer is licensing three in vivo autoimmune CAR-T programs from China's Starna Therapeutics. Adicon's planned $204 million purchase of Crown Biosciences fell through. Fierce's London Life Sciences Week piece describes a sector in good shape, with M&A strong and China a worry. In the UK, Ellipses Pharma is pushing a London listing, and its founder is calling for a capital gains tax cut to revive biotech listings. Danaher and Microsoft announced a partnership on smart lab instruments and AI tooling.

paragraphs.text: On policy, CMS proposed Medicare Advantage and Part D changes meant to increase competition. UnitedHealth and Aetna are now among the insurers suing over their 2027 star ratings, a sign of how much money rides on those scores. CMS is withdrawing its moratorium on new ACA broker registrations, which it imposed in September as part of an anti-fraud push. A Florida court tossed Tampa General's suit against Lilly over its 340B claims-data policy. A judge approved a $7 billion nationwide class settlement of Roundup cancer claims, which NYT says should end tens of thousands of lawsuits.

paragraphs.text: The AI selloff dominates. WSJ asks whether the bubble has already burst and says the recent decline looks a lot like the dot-com unwind. Anthropic's debut has not helped. WSJ says the stock slid on its second day and at one point traded just 5 cents above the IPO price, and that the company's record Thursday listing was followed a day later by a market rout. Bloomberg says Anthropic failed to calm AI jitters over the weekend. CNBC notes that unloved stocks such as Clorox, Boston Beer and Campbell's are being pitched as beneficiaries as the AI trade loses momentum, though that is one outlet's framing, not a verdict.

paragraphs.text: The stress is spreading in Asia. Bloomberg says China's AI stock trade has lost about $1.7 trillion and turned from a hot bet into a loser. Beijing cut margin requirements for stock financing to 80% to lift liquidity as leveraged trading declined. South Korea held an emergency meeting on Sunday and announced phased steps to calm volatile markets, including making sure its stock stabilization fund is ready. Policymakers are moving before Monday's open, which suggests they see real disorder. Two company items add to the AI picture. The NYT reports Nvidia is said to face an SEC probe into its accounting practices, with questions arising amid revelations about questionable chip sales in Asia. The FT says suppliers including Dell, HPE, Lenovo and Supermicro are raising AI server prices by up to 45% months after contracts were signed, hitting trading firms. The Nvidia report is secondhand and the excerpt gives no detail.

paragraphs.text: The rates picture is uncomfortable. The FT says the benchmark mortgage rate has risen above 7%, far from the 3% Donald Trump promised. MarketWatch says home sales are at a record low with prices at records, so the few buyers left are starting to negotiate hard. The FT also reports that Democrats led by Richard Neal want hearings to unwind Trump's tax and tariff measures, a political risk to watch. The FT's view that investors must unlearn the last 20 years on inflation, bonds and stocks fits the mood. It is one columnist's argument, not a forecast.

paragraphs.text: Commodities were jumpy. Bloomberg describes a week of squeezes and a meltdown in metals, with a bearish mood at the Shanghai copper gathering. The FT reports traders starting to ship US copper to China as tariff fears ease, because a shortage there and a high local premium create an arbitrage. In the Gulf, the FT says oil shipped through Hormuz fell as Iranian strikes increased, and an analyst calls the recovery in exports increasingly fragile. WSJ reports the UAE is shuttling oil past Iran with US military help to break Iran's hold on the waterway. Separately, a tentative deal averted a strike by security guards at the Los Angeles and Long Beach ports. Argentina's borrowing costs also jumped, which sits in the credit section.

paragraphs.text: The biggest financing item is SpaceX. Bloomberg reports that Goldman Sachs and Apollo priced $32 billion of SpaceX bonds to pay for AI chip purchases. It says Goldman spent more than a year working out how to fund chips without damaging corporate balance sheets. The excerpt gives no pricing or structure, but the size shows how much AI hardware spending is now being financed through debt markets. That matters more now because the equity side of AI is under strain and server costs are rising, as the FT reported.

paragraphs.text: Spreads were the other talking point. Traders Union relays Bob Elliott's argument that credit spreads are low, which suggests they might need to widen further before the Fed responds. That is one macro commentator's view. With equities falling and mortgage rates above 7%, the gap between calm credit and stressed stocks is worth watching. Sovereign credit showed more strain: the FT says Argentina's borrowing costs jumped as Javier Milei's falling approval and his financing plans rattled investors ahead of his re-election bid.

paragraphs.text: Private credit drew regulatory attention. Digg, summarizing other reporting, says the SEC and Treasury nominees reportedly brushed off private-credit worries. That is a thin source and the details are unclear, but it bears on how closely the sector will be supervised. Global Advisory Experts published guides on private credit in China, covering structures, filings and enforcement risk, and in Saudi Arabia, where it says the PIF's entry matters for lenders and borrowers. These read as advisory marketing and add little news. On the retail side, ETF Stream says Vanguard launched an active US high yield bond ETF. WSJ reports Mexican drug gangs are forcibly taking over small lenders and raising rates to diversify their income. That is an unusual risk for anyone exposed to Mexican microfinance.

paragraphs.text: Coverage of distress and leveraged loans was light today. Nothing in the list covers default rates, loan repricing or ratings actions.

The Anthropic IPO is the main deal story, and the post-mortems are not flattering. Reuters says that, like SpaceX, Anthropic ran an unusual process that chafed some bankers. Crypto Briefing says the record offering paid bankers well but left some frustrated by the terms. The FT asks whether Anthropic and its banks got a call wrong by exercising the greenshoe quickly, given the weak shares afterward. WSJ says the blame game has begun, and Finimize argues the deal showed who holds power on Wall Street. WSJ also profiles Dario and Daniela Amodei. The FT's note on big IPOs with small floats may relate, but the excerpt does not say. Taken together, issuers appear to be winning leverage over underwriters. Whether banks keep accepting that depends on how the stock trades.

paragraphs.text: The next listings are queuing up. The FT says Nscale is slowing hiring and curbing spending ahead of a planned $35 billion IPO, and falling AI valuations could complicate that plan. In Asia, Yuanji Food cleared its Hong Kong listing hearing, and Sinotau Pharmaceutical's retail tranche was oversubscribed more than 256 times. BusinessLine says 29 Indian companies are eyeing about ₹42,000 crore of IPOs before year-end as sentiment improves, though that was written before this weekend's Asian market moves. Leo Pharma's IPO delay is covered in the healthcare section.

paragraphs.text: Private equity brought some friction. The FT says co-investors in buyout funds are newly frustrated at being pushed out when assets are sold into continuation vehicles. Separately, CVC alleges accounting manipulation in Advent's €3 billion sale of Italian pastry ingredients business Irca, and Advent denies overstating Irca's performance. WSJ reports Nelson Peltz is trying to buy Wendy's again, but the CEO is standing in his way. Ardian, Heathrow's largest investor, told the FT it expects a third runway to be built. Another item reports a Series B startup acquired for 15 billion yuan, but the excerpt gives no buyer or detail. At DealBook, Elon Musk discussed a potential merger, but the list does not say which companies.

The outcome would set how much capital it must hold and could affect its strategy. In the US, the FT notes regulators are cutting executive pay disclosure at an awkward time. A guide on fintech M&A taxes in Indonesia rounds out a thin deal-flow day.
